opus-5.5.text:
I think about it a lot, actually. When I first got into machine learning research, I was drawn to questions that were more about understanding: why do neural networks work the way they do, what are they actually learning, what's going on under the hood with things like the lottery ticket hypothesis or how models generalize. Those questions felt intrinsically interesting to me, and I still find them really compelling.

But over time I've come to appreciate that understanding and practical impact aren't really in opposition. Often the best way to know whether you've truly understood something is to see whether that understanding lets you do something you couldn't do before: build a better method, predict when a model will fail, or design a training procedure that works more reliably. So I like research that sits in that middle ground, where you're asking a scientific question but the answer has some leverage on how people actually build and use these systems.

At the same time, I try not to let "practical impact" become a pressure that pushes me toward chasing benchmarks or incremental improvements just because they're easy to measure. Some of the most impactful work in the field started out looking pretty impractical. So my general approach is to follow what I'm genuinely curious about, but keep asking myself: if this works out, who would care, and what would it change? If I can't answer that at all, that's a sign I should rethink the direction. If I can, even if the payoff is a bit further down the road, then I feel comfortable pursuing it.

And especially now, with these models being deployed so widely, I think researchers have some responsibility to think about how their work connects to the real world, whether that's making models more reliable, more interpretable, or better at reasoning in ways people can trust. That feels like a meaningful kind of impact to aim for.

r002.rationale: The candidate describes a shift over time from pursuing intrinsically interesting questions toward also asking who would care and what the work would change, and says a direction with no answer may need rethinking.

fable-5.1.text:
I think about this a lot, honestly, because I came into research somewhat sideways. I spent time in industry before my PhD, working on problems where the question was always "does this actually move something?" And when I started doing research, I noticed there's a certain kind of pressure to pick one lane. Either you're doing the theory, the fundamental understanding stuff, or you're doing the applied, let's-ship-a-model work. And people sort of look at you funny if you want both.

My honest feeling is that I don't think practical impact should be the thing driving the choice of what to study, but it's a very good check on whether you're kidding yourself. A lot of my work has been about understanding why things work. The lottery ticket stuff, the generalization work, trying to figure out what's actually going on inside these models rather than just stacking more layers. And none of that was motivated by "this will make a product better next quarter." It was motivated by being confused and wanting to not be confused anymore.

But what I've found is that understanding tends to pay off practically, just on a delay. If you actually understand why a phenomenon happens, you end up with better intuitions for what will and won't work later, and that saves enormous amounts of compute and wasted effort down the line. So I don't see it as a tradeoff so much as a question of time horizon. The applied work is impact now. The understanding work is impact in two or three years, and it's less legible, which is the hard part.

Where I do push myself is to ask whether a question matters to anyone outside the small group of people who care about that exact question. If I can't articulate why someone building or using these systems would eventually care, that's a warning sign. Not a reason to stop necessarily, but a reason to think harder about why I'm doing it.

r001.rationale: The response says practical impact should not drive what she studies, but does not say that freedom from having to produce applied value attracted her to research.

r002.rationale: The response describes intellectual curiosity and later checking whether research matters beyond a small group, but does not say she came to question whether intellectual interest alone was sufficient after spending time researching.

astra-6.text: I think practical impact is something I’d like my research to have, but I don’t necessarily expect every project to have an immediate application. There’s value in stepping back and trying to understand something fundamental, even if you don’t yet know where that understanding will be useful. For me, it’s a balance: keeping real problems in mind while leaving room to follow questions that are interesting and might lead somewhere unexpected.
